q-12558:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 3x{e}^{2x+5}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=3 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{2x+5}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3x\cdot {e}^{2x+5}\,\text{d}x & =3x\cdot \frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{2}-\int \frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{2}\cdot 3\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3x{e}^{2x+5}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3x{e}^{2x+5}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{2x+5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3x{e}^{2x+5}}{2}-\frac{3{e}^{2x+5}}{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-14434:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 6x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=6x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=6 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{4x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 6x\cdot {e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x & =6x\cdot \frac{1}{4}{e}^{4x}-\int \frac{1}{4}{e}^{4x}\cdot 6\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6x{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}x{e}^{4x}-\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3x{e}^{4x}}{2}-\frac{3{e}^{4x}}{8}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-14451:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,v=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =2x\cdot (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-12565:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)\, & ⟹\,v=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We, substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)}{3})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)\text{d}x & =-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)}{3}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)}{9}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-74536:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 6 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 & -6 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 6 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 & -6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 6 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 & -6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & -2 & -6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-74604:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 5 & -7 & 17 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 5 & -7 & 17 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 8 & 17 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-8){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 40 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-135370:
The given matrix can be obtained from the identity matrix by permuting its columns. Therefore, $A$ is a permutation matrix.

The inverse of a permutation matrix can be found as follows: 

$$
{P}^{-1}={P}^{T}
$$

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-135391:
Notice that we're given a Frobenius matrix:

- all entries on the main diagonal are ones

- the matrix has only one column (the $2$nd column) where some entries below the main diagonal are not zeros

- all the other entries outside the main diagonal are zeros

To find the inverse of a Frobenius matrix, we simply take the non-zero entries outside the main diagonal with opposite signs. 

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-10662:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+y+z=2 \\ 0x+y-3z=1 \\ 0x+0y+0z=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since there are no such numbers $x,y,z$ that form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y+0z=-3,$ we can conclude that our system has no solution.

q-73958:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -6 & 8 \\ -2 & -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 12 & 18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -6 & 8 \\ 0 & -1 & -12 & 16 \\ 0 & 1 & 12 & 18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -6 & 8 \\ 0 & -1 & -12 & 16 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 34\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-2y-6z=8 \\ 0x-y-12z=16 \\ 0x+0y+0z=34\end{aligned}
$$

Since there are no such numbers $x,y,z$ that form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y+0z=34,$ we can conclude that our system has no solution.

q-4471:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=1$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x-1}{x-\sqrt{x}} & =\frac{1-1}{1-\sqrt{1}}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x-1}{x-\sqrt{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{(x-\sqrt{x})(x+\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{{x}^{2}-{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{{x}^{2}-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{x(x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x+\sqrt{x}}{x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{1+\sqrt{1}}{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-34153:
We say that three vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

The equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ corresponds to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system, we create its augmented matrix and reduce it using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we conclude that the basic variables are ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$, while ${x}_{3}$ is the free variable. 

Since there is one free variable, the equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ has an infinite number of nonzero solutions, which means that the vectors are linearly dependent. 

Therefore, statements I and III are false, while statement II is true.

q-70827:
We need a vector $v=⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $r\cdot ⟨1,2,-1⟩=7$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨1,2,-1⟩.$ So, $v⊥n$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,2,-1⟩ & =0 \\ {t}_{1}+2{t}_{2}-{t}_{3} & =0 \\ {t}_{3} & ={t}_{1}+2{t}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain 

$$
v=⟨{t}_{1},\,{t}_{2},\,{t}_{1}+2{t}_{2}⟩,
$$

where ${t}_{1},{t}_{2}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

We are told that the first component of $v$ equals $0.$ So, we must set ${t}_{1}=0.$ 

Since $v$ is nonzero, we can pick any ${t}_{2}\ne 0.$ For example, setting ${t}_{2}=1$, we get

$$
v=⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩.
$$

Therefore, $\frac{b}{c}=\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, $\frac{b}{c}=\frac{1}{2}.$

q-73612:
Remember that the pivots of a matrix in row echelon form are the first non-zero entries in each row of the matrix.

We can see that $B$ has $3$ pivots in the $1$st, $3$rd and $5$th columns:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the only non-pivot columns are the $2$nd and $4$th columns.

q-73638:
First, we need to convert $P$ to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 5 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & -4 & 5 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & ↔{R}_{4} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & -4 & 5 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the row echelon form, we see that $P$ has $4$ pivots. In particular, the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, $3$rd, and $4$th columns.
